utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first matter is this: We have prepared a schedule of sittings through until the beginning of September and copies are available for that from the Senior Legal Officer. The next matter is this: We have, as I understand it, these matters to consider, and I propose, briefly, to set out the agenda. There may be other matters too, but the outstanding matters are these: I'm going to give a brief ruling on the international armed conflict documents. We will then deal with the Kiseljak binder, the video evidence, the affidavits, the transcripts, any other outstanding Prosecution material, and at the end, we will spend a little time on some housekeeping to make sure that matters are in order. Turning to the international armed conflict binders, we've already said that we will admit them, but I think I should add this: that in doing so, we are applying the same principles in relation to admissibility as those we apply to the admissibility of the documents when ruling on the outstanding exhibits. The objections related to hearsay, lack of foundation, and authenticity, signature, or relevance, or indeed other objections, are all matters which go to the weight of the evidence and not to its admissibility. However, only legible exhibits will be admitted and those with translations in one of the languages of the Tribunal. There is one matter which I want to raise about those exhibits, and that is in relation to Exhibit 2436, conveniently can be found in the Defence objections, and it states -- the objection states that material from the report has been redacted. Now, it would be of assistance, before ruling on that document, to know what the position is. It may be convenient if we return to that during the course of the morning. Mr. Scott, if you could let me know what the position about that document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go on to the Kiseljak binder. In relation to that, we shall apply the principles which we set out in our written ruling in relation to the Tulica binder; that is, we will exclude witness statements and investigators' reports. We will admit exhibits, that is, photographs, and videos, maps, death certificates, and exhumation reports. I take it that all the transcripts which are referred to in the report or binder have been ruled on, and unless there are any other matters outstanding, I think that that covers the binder. I should say that we have taken into account the binder itself, of course, and the documents in it, and also the Defence objections which are set out in their document which we've had in front of us; and applying the Tulica ruling, that would be our ruling about that binder. Are there any other outstanding matters, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. On Kiseljak, if it please the Court, I was simply going to add that I think that the revised binders, in the past couple weeks, have been revised binders now down to two volumes, and with a new index and an exactly -- as far as I know, exactly parallels the Court's ruling. It now contains the index, exhibit materials, no investigator's report, no statements. So to the best of my knowledge, the revised binders, two volumes, are completely consistent with the Court's rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Browning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would simply ask that the Prosecution confirm that all material has been provided to us. According to our records, there are certain documents set out in the binder that we have not received. Moreover, there were some documents that were produced on February 25th, and there were no translations provided in connection with those additional documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I confirm what I said earlier, Your Honour. I think there were one or two documents which were removed from the list, for whatever reason; either legible copies could not be found, so they were simply removed from the index and the material, or there had originally been a wrong number and it was like the next number, two numbers later, so that the index was changed to correct that. But as far as I know, the binders that I'm now looking at or have before me for Kiseljak are the final binders that have resolved, to the best of our ability, all the outstanding objections raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would simply propose the opportunity to review that and sit down with the Prosecution and point out the documents we have specific concerns about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next matter concerns the video evidence. The position is this: that we have now been provided with an amended Prosecution document. By my calculation, there are 41 videos in the document, and analysing it, some 17 are of interviews of various people, 7 of press conferences, 6 of ceremonies or public events, 3 of damage, and there are 8 of other matters, miscellaneous, but that does include reports, the sort of which we have been admitting during the trial. I must say, speaking for myself, these are all the sort of items which we have admitted during the trial, applying the principles with regard to hearsay evidence which we have done and which we've frequently set out. That is, that matters of foundation and absence of foundation and absence of authentication are matters which go to the weight, and these are the sort of items which speak for themselves. But perhaps I could start with the Prosecution. You were going to go through the videos with the Defence. I hope that's been done and that this is now in final form.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Mr. President. Personally, I counted 42 extracts, not 41. Perhaps that was a mistake I made. These are extracts that come from 16 video cassettes, and some extracts come from that same cassette. As of today, we have presented to this Trial Chamber 28 extracts which were played here. They came, according to our estimates, from 17 different cassettes. Therefore, there are 42 extracts that we would have liked to present to the Trial Chamber, but for time reasons we were not able to do that. And we considered this week to present four extracts that are ready and are available to you, if you want them, as regards the extracts for which there are transcripts, because obviously there are some extracts which, as you said, which speak for themselves. They are just pictures, and there's no need to have a transcript. The images are sufficiently clear. As regards the transcript, we reviewed it thoroughly. Unless I made a mistake, we think that we gave to the Defence all those transcripts which correspond to the cassettes which are listed here and for which, in fact, there was a need to have transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I think you'll find the number is 41. It was 42 originally. I may be wrong, and correct me if I am. Two were then removed and, I think, one added in the new list, so the number should be 41. It seems to meet with some agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that you're right, Mr. President. On my list, there's still 42 extracts, but I'm sure that you have a complete list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lopez-Terres, as regards the transcripts, I think that whatever the situation, the transcripts must be exhaustive, because we, from a practical point of view -- well, first we've got to look at the transcripts before we can look at the images, and it's from the transcripts that we can know exactly what it's about. Obviously, if there is no sound, then you're right, but you're only right in that case, if there's no sound, if it's silent films. But insofar as there is sound, we need the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, according to information that I have, and we worked last week on that transcripts question, unless I made a mistake, all the corresponding transcripts were submitted and they are complete. What can happen sometimes is that the translation of a cassette deals with several events, and some of the events are not those that we consider relevant for this case, so on the same page you might have part of a transcript which is not part of something that's of interest to us. That's simply because the Translation Service used a joint document for several conversations or several events, but there's no selection that we made in the transcript. When it's submitted, it's submitted in full. The Defence already received the transcripts in question. That was recently, and the Trial Chamber now is being given the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, let me say this before you begin: that we have your document setting out your objections, and of course there's a number which you haven't yet received, and I hope you've had the opportunity of going through the matter and reviewing it with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, let me say that I have made every request possible to meet with the Prosecution and to resolve as many of these differences as possible. Unfortunately, no such meeting has taken place. I would like to say that we have analysed the list that we received yesterday, and with the assistance of the usher, I would like to distribute our position now that we have additional information from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why has no meeting taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the hearing on Wednesday, March 1, I, at the end of the day, asked Mr. Lopez-Terres if we might be able to meet. The next day, a letter was sent to Mr. Lopez-Terres when the meeting did not take place. The following day, on Friday, Mr. Sayers sent a letter to Mr. Nice, requesting a meeting. Sunday evening, we received yet the sixth list of OTP videos. It is an ever-changing list, and what happened was we got this list of 40-plus videos and a stack of transcripts. And what we had to do, even though we had requested them to simply provide us with the exhibits so we could easily tell what we were dealing with -- the mess that we were given on Sunday evening was a list of videos, and we were told to go to our video library, videos that we had previously received from the Prosecution, and take a two- or three-hour tape and, using the transcript, try to determine what portion they are now considering to be their exhibits. It has required a tremendous amount of time on my part and on the part of my staff. I apologise that we are objecting to numerous videos, but it is not without trying, on the Defence's part, to work this issue out. As it stands right now, there are still ten videos that we have never received from the Prosecution. We have made numerous and repeated requests to receive the information, but it simply hasn't been coming to us. This seems to be a never-ending process with the Prosecution with respect to the videos. As I understand what Mr. Lopez-Terres is saying, there is still more changes yet to come, and there has to be closure on this issue. We are in the process of trying to prepare our various motions, and we need to know what the evidence is that the Court will consider or the evidence that becomes part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. Mr. Lopez-Terres, why did a meeting not take place? It was the clear order of the Court, or, at the very least, a request, that there should be such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wasn't myself present when those instructions were given. I was informed that the Chamber wanted contacts to be taken with the Defence. I myself was very present in the courtroom this week, as you know. I was not in the position to speak with the Defence, and Mr. Browning was not always here. Once again, I would say that further to the request that was made, we performed a final analysis of all the cassettes for which we had transcripts, and we submitted to the Defence, through those lists that you know now but which the Defence knew already, our last position when the cassettes were given. And those that remained and those -- and the transcripts were pending, we gave our opinion about all of them. There is a clarification that should be made. Formerly, when we would present to the Chamber extracts, we wanted to present only an extract. The difficulty was that the Defence wanted each time to have the entire cassette from which the extract came. The cassette would have many other extracts that had nothing to do with what we were attempting to present, and therefore the Defence found itself, on several occasions, with cassettes which had extracts that we were not planning to show, extracts that were shown later, and the cassettes had exhibit numbers which were different depending on the case, and, in fact, this did cause some difficulty on their part. However, I would say it was the request of the Defence, that wanted to be sure that we would not present the extracts that could have been fabricated or truncated, and that's why we gave the entire cassettes each time, which perhaps may have contributed to the confusion in which the Defence finds itself now. But that was not what we had intended to do at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, with no effort to repeat what Mr. Lopez-Terres has said. There was, I understand -- I was not present in the meeting. I understand there was a meeting toward the latter part of February. Subsequent to that meeting, there have been extensive exchange of correspondence. So let me just clarify to the Court, and whether we're in agreement or disagreement with the Defence on this, I guess I'm not sure, but I would say to the Court there has been extensive communication between the parties on this issue. Any suggestion that there has not been is in error. There has been an effort to present this in the most -- which admittedly is some difficult material because of the way that it was originally presented to the OTP by way of these composite tapes, but there's been a concerted effort to simplify, as far as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is not whether there has been extensive consultation over a period of time. The question is whether, subsequent to the order made by the president, there has been the consultation that the Chamber required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only say that I believe there was. I was not personally -- as the Court may understand, none of us, on any of the teams, I suspect, do everything, but my understanding is that there has been extensive consultation up to and including the past several days. The submission -- the index that the Court has in front of it that was given out a few minutes ago was provided -- this last further version -- I don't want there to be any impression there weren't any prior versions. This last current version was submitted to the Defence on Sunday with the material -- with these excerpts and items attached. They are cross-referenced by number. The items have markings on them as to which excerpt they relate to: 26.1, et cetera. They are provided with the chart. So, Your Honour, I guess all I can say is we have tried. We've made a good-faith effort. We think we have done it, Judge Robinson, pursuant to the Court's instruction. Perhaps not perfectly, perhaps not completely to the Defence's satisfaction, but we have made the best effort. I think that's where it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Browning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would respectfully disagree with the statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't want to hear about this. Now, let's get on with it. What is the position now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are currently 10 videotapes that we have not received, a eleventh videotape we cannot decipher what it is the Prosecution is referring to. There are several tapes that are incomplete, and the transcripts are incomplete. In one tape, for example, there are 47 places where -- 46 places where the transcript reads "incomprehensible" and seven times when it reads "interruption," and there are various other documents, videotapes that have not been transcribed. Your Honour, our position is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If in the transcript there is something which is not comprehensible, then it's just incomprehensible. That's it. This is not a reason for not admitting the cassette. It is possible that the cassette technically may not be very audible, that is, one does not hear it well, and that would be indicated in the transcript; that's all. But as we said, this has to do with the weight that should be given to this or that document, but it is not a question of admissibility. The problem, in fact, which arises now for you is to settle some purely technical problems with the Prosecutor, because as regards admissibility, there should be no difficulty in admitting a cassette. We still have to know whether that does, in fact -- in effect, that is the cassette that you need. If there is a proper correspondence between the cassette and the transcript there, then there would only be technical problems that arise, and those are the problems that have to be settled. Can we agree as to the admissibility of the evidence on the basis of what was just said by the president, that principle, and I ask that you settle technical problems amongst yourselves, because we cannot continually go back to the technical problem and wasting time and the Tribunal's resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I certainly very much agree, and the tape that I'm referring to we have a transcript of but have never been provided the video. So until we have the opportunity to see the video, we can't determine the accuracy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see what you've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Browning, you can help us with this? Do you accept any of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us know what you accept, please. Let's go through what you accept. At least it will start clearing the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Okay. Exhibit 117. On page 1. I'm sorry, Your Honour. On page 4, 1280.2 was admitted on the 6th of March, 2000, according to our records. On page 6, 1361.1. That video was first identified yesterday, but we have no objection otherwise than the untimely designation. On page 7, 2126. Ms. Bower has indicated that that was previously admitted as Z1167, and assuming that's the case, we would have no objection. Same page, 2258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, going through the objections, you refer to one which you don't say you've received at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: The videos that we have not received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: The videos we have not received are Z26; 26.1; 26.2; 26.3; 431.1; 478, which, if I'm not mistaken, I think 478 might have been removed from the list yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I apologise for that. 528.1, 548.3, 652, and 1786. The one video that we still cannot decipher from our tapes what the Prosecution is referring to is 1298. The reason we can't decipher that is I believe there was no translation provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, there is something in your objection where you mention that it is in contravention of Trial Chamber's timetable order directing that outstanding exhibits be produced by 28th of January, 2000. For example, I think number 1428. And there are others, 2602 and so on. Can you explain exactly what is the meaning of this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understood the Court's timetabling order, there was to be a time period so that the Prosecution would identify the outstanding exhibits so we wouldn't be in this situation at the tail end of the case, having to waste the Tribunal's time on these sort of issues. If the Trial Chamber decides to change that scheduling order or determine it's not applicable to videos, in that particular case we would have no objection, but we are in this situation because the designation of the videos is coming to us at the tail end of the case, and we would do our best to work through it; it's just been very difficult, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, given the general principles that we have laid down, given the fact that the case is coming to an end, what is your submission? What do you ask us to do about these?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the videos that we have not received or have not been provided information from the Prosecution so we can identify the segments that they intend to use, we ask that they be excluded from evidence. With respect to the tapes where the video and audio are incomplete, we certainly understand the position of the Trial Chamber that in some cases no one can do anything to the contrary to determine if there is better quality tape out there. It is surprising, however, that there are so many tapes that cut in and out and there are gaps in the tape, but I understand there is nothing that we might able to do along those lines. I note our objection on that, and I guess it's really a -- what will be the ground rules for use of videos in this case. Can a video be admitted if there are gaps in the video? And I guess there are two other categories of documents that we object to. I understand the Trial Chamber's position, but I do think it's worth giving a specific example of what I see as nothing more than a witness statement that is in the form of video, and that is 1281.1. This is Nelson Draper, an officer from CanBat, who is talking about an investigation concerning Stupni Do. He proceeds to begin the tape by describing that this tape shall only be used on a need-to-know basis, and he explains the limitations in his investigation, and then he proceeds to describe things such as what a 4-year-old child proceeded to tell an unnamed woman, who then, in turn, told someone within CanBat or UNPROFOR. So you have multiple levels of hearsay, and we have never had the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Draper concerning that investigation or his statement, which is essentially coming into evidence through this video. I would submit that it is not in accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal dealing with affidavit statements of witnesses. It does not -- we are precluded from our right of confrontation with regard to the statements that Mr. Draper makes, and he was never even designated as a witness. There are two other tapes which fall within that category: 2544, 342.4, and one other, 1292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page is that, 342.4?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: It would be on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with 342.4. You say "a broadcast on Serbian TV." You say in here it would be unreliable. That's purely a matter of weight, isn't it? But you go on to say "contains a witness statement." What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, basically it is a Serbian army scout testifying on Serbian TV about -- basically, the statement is made by this witness that the HVO asked Serbs to shell a particular location. We have been denied the opportunity to cross-examine that witness. I think it would be unfair for this clip to come into evidence without the opportunity of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: 1292, which is on page 5. And I'll also note 2544, which is on page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with 1292. Again, you say this is Serbian TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say it's Serbian TV; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But again that's a point which has got to be considered. And what is the witness statement here?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: The witness statement concerns Mr. Kordic, if I recall. I would need to pull the specific transcript, which could be done fairly quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Browning, as regards your last objection, are these interviews which were distributed or did they come from the archives? Because there's a difference between an interview which was distributed or broadcast to the public, which became a public thing which was seen by other people, and other interviews which remained in the archives. If I've understood you correctly, these are interviews that were broadcast over television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: With respect to this specific example, 1292, if you consider Serbian TV to be a reliable source, presumably it was broadcast over television to the public by Serbian TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem, you see, is that from the time that a video was broadcast, it becomes evidence insofar as it had an impact on the public. It's not the -- by the fact that it had impact it is no longer a private thing but, rather, public information, such as information found in a newspaper or any other information distributed to the public. It's a different thing between information which is broadcast to the public and information which remains confidential within an institution. Therefore, from the time it has been distributed to the public, it's known and it's going to have an effect on that public, so as such, it's of interest to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to your question, it is 1281.1 would be the one video among those four that I've been discussing which would not be available to the public. The other three appear to be broadcasts made to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you're going to deal -- you dealt with 1292, and did you have one other? Mr. Lopez-Terres, we'll hear you at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: The other one is 2544, which is on page 7. This is a broadcast, or appears to be a broadcast. It is undated by the Prosecution, but it is my understanding the broadcast was made seven months after the events in Stupni Do. In that situation, I believe it would be beyond the indictment period, and I would submit that would have no bearing upon the public's reaction to this particular broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there's anything else that you want to add, we'll hear from Mr. Cerkez' Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: The only thing else that I would add, Your Honour, with respect to the transcripts that have just been distributed, if they are identical to the transcripts that I received, what takes place is you have a half a page of transcript, followed by what the Prosecution intends to designate as the "Z" number. I would submit it would be more appropriate to remove the portion of those transcripts that are not part of the Prosecution exhibit. Otherwise, it will simply create confusion in the record, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that they contain -- what do you say they contain, Mr. Browning? Let me see if I follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I was trying to -- as I understand the way the Prosecution has laid out the transcripts, they transcribe a tape in its entirety, then choose to use a portion of that tape as an exhibit. So if you look in your transcript book, you will see several pages of transcription and then a "Z" designation written into the margin. The one that I'm looking at, you have three quarters of a page and then you see the words "Z419.2." So three quarters of the page has no bearing upon the exhibit being introduced, is extraneous, in some cases contains separate material that would be objectionable, and it would be better to simply clearly designate the transcript for the specific videos at issue without including extraneous material either before or after those transcripts of the Prosecution videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The Cerkez Defence has been following this list. This list has been narrowed down, and practically all video material that would be related to evidence, even such poor and insufficient evidence against the co-accused Mario Cerkez, is now eliminated. However, in principle, we oppose the introduction of videotapes as evidence in this way. We believe that they can be introduced only with the assistance of a witness who recognises the recorded scene in a way, describes it, confirms it. Also, we need information about the person who did the filming, where, when, and it is only at such a point that that kind of videotape can have corroborative value related to other pieces of evidence. I don't think there's any point in my elaborating this point any further. I just wish to add one more than thing, lest I be misunderstood by the Court. There has been an enormous amount of video material during discovery. Recently, we gave up on following this entire story, because we got a video from the Prosecutor and in one clip it seemed that Arnold Schwarzenegger, the actor, belonged to the HVO forces. And we viewed this 15 times, and when we realised what this was and when we came to the conclusion that we could not confirm whether this was filmed by the BBC or not and this was BBC material, to tell you the truth, we gave up on the entire thing. We saw that there was no evidence against Cerkez, and we think that it is not worth all this time and effort. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To respond directly to what Mr. Kovacic said, I see that he's got a lot of humour, first of all. It was never claimed by the Office of the Prosecutor that Mr. Schwarzenegger was part of the HVO. I suppose that was a comment that the journalist made and that it's become common language now that somebody who was covered with munitions and weapons is either called "Schwarzenegger" or "Rambo". That's just part of the way people talk today. But that doesn't mean that the Office of the Prosecutor has to add the people who were being -- as people being prosecuted here, Arnold Schwarzenegger. As regards what Mr. Kovacic said, he did say that for each cassette, he wanted somebody to come to identify it, et cetera. And I would say if the Tribunal is going to become the tribunal of every journalist in the world, then we're prepared to do so, but I'm afraid that's going to take a great deal of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't trouble about that argument. It's the hearsay argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But perhaps you might deal with the detailed argument that Mr. Browning put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would simply like to say, and this is an illustration of what I was explaining a few minutes ago more specifically, perhaps, for Judge Bennouna, that the transcripts that were transmitted to the Defence are transcripts that we have, and they also have OTP reference numbers. The Translation Service at this Tribunal, which does not come under the authority of the OTP, let me remind you, translated the cassettes successively. And this is why on this document, for example, that the Defence mentioned a few minutes ago, Z442.4, which I would like to say, in passing, it doesn't only talk about the Serbian army but the Jajce Brigade, there are several translations, several transcriptions, and, in fact, the top part has nothing to do with the extract that we are asking the Trial Chamber to review. If the OTP had understood that that extract would also be taken into consideration, an exhibit number would have been attributed to it. There was no bad faith or any attempt on the part of the Prosecutor to fool people and to push through documents, but it was simply the fact that it was on the same page. There are only transcripts for which there are reference numbers. If the Chamber wants, in order to avoid any misunderstandings, assuming that there was a misunderstanding, wants us to cut out the upper or lower parts and that you consider only the transcript which more specifically deals with the extract from the cassette, we can do that. But it's self-evident that only the extract with a reference number is the one that we are asking review of. As regards the second exhibit which was mentioned by the Defence a few minutes ago, that is, Z1292, it has been presented in the same way. This is the logo of the television in Croatia, and Mr. Ivica Rajic, the HVO commander in Kiseljak, is giving interview, and the interview was given to Serbian television or French television or Croatian television. In general, in order to finish with this argument, it seems to us that the all the problems which are raised by the Defence through the chart that has been established or Mr. Browning's comments this morning, these are problems that are not part of admission of exhibits, whether they be transcripts or extracts, but simply a problem of weight which is to be given by the Trial Chamber and the probative value that the Trial Chamber will give to the various documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider this, of course, and give you our ruling after the adjournment. utterances.text: Just as a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had overlooked that. Do you want to add anything of your own?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I propose not to add anything to the matter that's already stated in our papers. They speak for themselves, but just a brief response to the document we received yesterday from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It seems to me that the Prosecution is saying, "We would like the Court to admit these seven affidavits," and there's another one, which have been submitted to us. The same arguments apply to it. utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I would like to join everything that my learned friend Mr. Sayers has said, and I believe that this is not just a technical matter, but I think that the question of admission of affidavits is of essential importance because these documents can be very important. We do not think that this Rule can be a lex specialis. That's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mikulicic, could you tell us very briefly how you understand 94 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very pleased to do that. Mr. Cerkez's Defence and I myself interpret Rule 94 ter just as it is formulated, which means that an affidavit or another formal statement may be used in the proceedings as supporting material in relation to a fact which is contested and which is referred to by a witness. Such material must be delivered to the Defence before the witness examination, and the Defence should have an opportunity to lodge an objection and it should have seven days in which to do so. Therefore, affidavits may not be admitted as part of a package but only as supporting material, along with a live witness testifying in court. This procedure simply has not been complied with by the Prosecution. The Prosecution submitted several affidavits and wished to submit them as exhibits, just as it did the village binders and some other materials. However, this is not the procedure prescribed by Rule 94 ter. I hope that I have answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly. We would rely mainly on the skeleton argument that was presented to Your Honours. Just a couple of points. It seems to us that maybe our submission wasn't clearly understood by the Defence. We have never tried to invent a new rule. We have never tried to ignore that. Unfortunately, and due to the practical problems that we have faced in finding a procedure suitable for the national authorities in Bosnia and for the parties, we were not in a position to meet the timely requirements of Rule 94 ter. What we have said is that nonetheless, the affidavits or former statements are corroborative in nature, they all address facts in dispute, and that the unfortunate possibility of complying with the timely requirements doesn't cause a fatal prejudice or any sort of prejudice at all, actually, to the Defence in this case, and that the Chamber will be in a position to be indulgent to the Prosecution, mindful of the practical problems obtaining these affidavits have caused. And in the event that that Chamber considered that the timing requirements for 94 ter are essential, the Chamber will still have the power to admit these affidavits under Rule 89(C). That was the core of our submission. Apart from that, we have nothing more to add to our skeleton argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider these two matters now. We will take the coffee break. We will sit again at quarter to, unless you hear to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I deal first with the video evidence, beginning by saying, as I did at the outset, that we have admitted videos in this case. Very often, they speak for themselves. However, there are occasionally matters which give rise to concerns about authentication and the like, and our ruling reflects that. I would also add this: that, of course, very often what's on a video isn't hearsay evidence at all; it's merely an evidence of fact. For instance, public ceremonies, proclamations, that sort of thing. All that's being shown is what actually occurred, and so there's no breach of any hearsay rule, if such existed here. First of all, those -- and I will deal with this by way of number, the exhibit number as on the Prosecution list -- first of all, those admissible, not objected to and already admitted, 117, 419.2, 1280.2, 1298, 1361.1, 2126, 2258. The next category to be admitted are those of public broadcasts, because once an item is broadcast, it is in the public domain, it becomes a fact. This was the broadcast which may or may not have an effect upon the public, but it's also something which is admissible of the broadcast itself, and the fact that it's public gives it added authenticity. Under this heading, admissible are 255, 342, 342.2, 342.5, 419, 1185, 1280.3, 1292, and 1356.1. In the same category are the press conferences, 173, 235, 562, and the public ceremonies, 330, 1186. The following are excluded; first of all, those not provided to the Defence: 26, 26.1, 26.2, 26.3, 431.1, 528.1, 625, and 1786. We accept too the Defence submissions that where, in effect, what is happening is that the broadcast or the video -- in one case not a broadcast at all but for confidential consumption; that is, Mr. Draper's broadcast is, in effect, the giving of evidence by a witness not subject to cross-examination and not subject to oath, and that, of course, in effect, is evidence without cross-examination and amounts to hearsay, controversial, and of a sort which, in our view, should be excluded as too prejudicial to be admitted without cross-examination. 1281.1 and 2544 are in that category. We also exclude matters outside the indictment: 1428, 2482. We also exclude as incomplete or merely evidence which it appears to us not to be probative, in some cases interviews: 342.3, an interview with Roso; 457.1, 1315.6, another interview with Roso; 1322, an interview with Kostroman, and the date is unclear; 1347, another interview with Kostroman, 1347.2, 1390, 2238, 2602. I turn next to the affidavit evidence. The Prosecution seek to have admitted the evidence of eight affidavits under Rule 94 ter, the terms of which I will refer to briefly. To prove a fact in dispute, a party may propose to call a witness and to submit, in corroboration of his or her testimony on that fact, affidavits or formal statements signed by other witnesses in accordance with the law and procedure of the State in which such affidavits or statements are signed. These affidavits or statements are admissible provided they are filed prior to the giving of testimony by the witness to be called and the other party does not object within seven days after completion of testimony of the witness through whom the affidavits are tendered. If the party objects and the Trial Chamber so rules, or if the Trial Chamber so orders, the witnesses shall be called for cross-examination. To this application, the Defence object. I say the Defence submissions were made by Mr. Kordic in writing, to which Mr. Cerkez joins. The objections which are made are in this form: First of all, it's said that the affidavits or formal statements should be taken in accordance with the law and procedure of the State in which they are signed. This, they say, say the Defence, is a procedure only available to States, and therefore to admit the affidavits would violate the principle of equality of arms. The Prosecution point out, on the other hand, that the Defence may seek the assistance of the Trial Chamber to obtain affidavits, and in Aleksovski they were able to do so; and I can say that in Kupreskic too, affidavits on behalf of the Defence were admitted. That seems to us to be a sensible submission. There is no breach of the equality of arms here. It is open to the Defence, as I have said, to obtain these affidavits, and if not, they can certainly apply to the Trial Chamber for their assistance. The second objection is that the affidavits must be supplied, according to the Rule, to the other party before the principal witness testifies. The Defence point out that to meet this requirement, they would have had to hold back witnesses until virtually the end of the case, important witnesses, and they also point out that there is no prejudice to the accused. The Trial Chamber, in this connection, observed that Rules must be interpreted to give them useful effect. This is a principle of international law, expressed in French as: “l'interpretation par la methode de la faire utile”, and also in the Latin maxim: ut res magis valeat quam pereat. And this reference to this principle may be found in the Chorzow Factory case, 1927, Permanent Court of Justice, the Corfu Channel case, 1950, International Court of Justice. The Trial Chamber applies this principle to the Rule, and our Rule holds here that the admission of these statements is not prevented by Rule 94 ter. To do so would be to rule that a technical procedural requirement, if it were right, would certainly lead to or may lead to a defeat to the interests of justice. We note, finally, that no prejudice to the accused can be occasioned by the admission, at this stage, of the affidavits. The Defence have had the affidavits for some time and have been able to make their detailed submissions. I'm told that the Corfu Channel case was in 1949. The next objection is that Rule 94 ter didn't envisage the use which has been made of it in this particular case, that is, validating witness statements from some time ago. The Prosecution respond that this was the only practical course; namely, to have the witness approve and swear to the original witness statement, that witnesses here were prepared to make and did make changes to their statements, and that if this course wasn't followed, the Rule would be impractical. The Trial Chamber observed that there is no practical reason why this procedure should not be followed and that a witness should not look at his or her statement and swear that it's the truth. So that reason does not find favour. The next objection is that the Rule anticipates that there is a live witness whose evidence on a specific fact is corroborated by the affidavit in question, and in this case there was no live witness. The Prosecution, in response, say that the evidence in the affidavits is, in fact, corroborative and that the term of “fact in dispute” should be given a broad interpretation. I turn, in those circumstances, to the particular witnesses and deal, first of all, with Mujo Alispahic. He gives evidence about Rijeka and Dubravica. In this connection, I would say that the Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution's submission about this is correct, that all that is required is that there should be some confirmation or support of evidence in a very general sense and that the term "facts in dispute" should be given a very broad interpretation. There's evidence of Dubravica from Abdulah Ahmic; Payam Akhavan, from Rijeka; Sulejman Kavazovic, and Witness L. There's evidence about trench-digging from Witness U, Fuad Zeco, Mirsad Ahmic. We turn next to Nusreta Hrustic. She gives evidence about Gacice -- again I'm summarising this very generally -- about the attack on Gacice, and about Mr. Kordic's appearance on television. Again, there is evidence in this case, a great deal of evidence, about television appearances by Mr. Kordic, for instance, by Nusreta Mahmutovic, Anto Breljas, Witness Q, and there's evidence about the attack on Gacice from Mr. Morsink, Witness V, and the transcript of Major Friis-Pedersen. I turn next to Sedzad Hrustic. He gives evidence about Mr. Kordic being at an oath-taking, and he also gives evidence about events in the cinema. There is, it's pointed out by the Defence, no evidence of Mr. Kordic being present at the cinema in any of the rest of the evidence. However, given the broad interpretation that I said we should, there is much evidence that Mr. Kordic was in Vitez; Witness Z, for instance, and Anto Breljas. There is much evidence about the cinema, and, in those circumstances, we're satisfied that this criterion is approved -- is met, I should say. The next witness is one whom I'm not going to name. She was subjected to sexual attack in the cinema, she says. There is, it's pointed out by the Defence, no evidence of such attacks in the cinema. However, evidence was given by Witness S of such attacks in the area of Vitez, and in those circumstances the criterion is met. Salih Sadibasic, evidence about Mr. Kordic on television. Again, I've covered that. Vasvija Kermo gives evidence about Loncari and Jelinak. Again, there is substantial evidence on both those topics, that is, the attacks on those villages. Mr. Kavazovic, Witness H, Witness T, Witness A, Witness O, and Witness J both deal with Loncari, Jelinak, and also, I should mention, Merdani. Number 7 is Mr. Morsink. His affidavit arises in this way: that he said in his original statement that a list was supplied to him of detainees. The list was supplied by the HVO in Vitez. He was given that list. He did not mention that in his evidence. It arose as a matter in dispute. Therefore, it was suggested that an affidavit be supplied. In this case, there is much evidence about the detention in the cinema. This list is a list of detainees which is admissible. Finally, the statement of Mr. Causevic, the affidavit of Mr. Causevic. He gives evidence about Vitez and Dubravica school. Again, there is much evidence on all those matters. The vet station, evidence was given by Mr. Fuad Zeco. There was evidence, much evidence about Mr. Kraljevic and on the relationship between Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Kraljevic. Angus Hay, Anto Breljas, and Lee Whitworth gave evidence. Likewise, there is much evidence, which I will not enumerate, on Mr. Miroslav Bralo. For those reasons, the submission that there is no live witness giving the evidence which this is corroborative of, that submission is rejected. Finally, we have to consider, in light of the Defence objections, whether there should be cross-examination of the witnesses. We have considered that. We do not think that that is required or necessary in this case. We think that the matter is covered by the affidavit being on oath. But when we come to consider this evidence, we will, of course, bear in mind that it was not given subject to cross-examination. Yes. We turn to the next matters, and I think the next matter is the transcripts. Mr. Scott, were you going to deal with those?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The confidential witness, of course, you can address us on; Mr. Kaiser, without much encouragement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT

utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we're getting toward the end and the hour is short, and I know the Court's view on this, but if the Court will allow me literally about three minutes concerning Dr. Kaiser. I do think it's an important point, and I think it can be quickly covered, and the Court can certainly be in a position to rule quickly, but I ask the Court to just give us a few minutes to at least try to persuade the Court as to our position on this issue. If I could ask the usher to hand to the Court. Copies of this were provided to Defence counsel yesterday, but for ease of reference, if you want to provide an additional copy today, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we understood the Court's -- well, two things. To set the scene, the objection to Dr. Kaiser's transcript coming in when we were dealing with these issues more extensively a few weeks ago was largely on the basis, at least from the Defence, that that was in the nature of an expert witness, who had not been properly presented to the Court as such. And the Court's own ruling, it appeared that the Court gave substantial weight or consideration to the fact that the Court considered the items to the proof to be cumulative. Let me say that what we have done, Your Honour, what we asked the Court to consider, is some very -- a limited amount of Dr. Kaiser's testimony. I have handed the Court now two documents. One I'll just -- I'll just start with the one page entitled "Kaiser Evidence." The Court will see we have been, I think, extremely selective as to a portion of the transcript, a total of some 33 pages, and certain exhibits that accompany those portions of the transcript. What the other document does, Your Honour, the chart, the other chart that is some two pages, to give some further idea as to what this testimony covers and the issue of cumulativeness, Your Honour, what this does is indicate on the left side the particular location addressed by Mr. Kaiser. We submit that in these portions he is not providing expert opinion; he is simply saying, "I was at such locations and observed this damage." He is essentially a contemporary observer at these locations. For instance, as an example, Loncari mosque. He was at the mosque. It was destroyed by a charge. He talks about that at pages 6 -- 10614 to 10615. There is a photograph of that. Then that's a quick summary, Your Honour. In terms of whether the evidence is cumulative or not, Your Honour, we reviewed the evidence to date, or at least up until the last week or so in the case, and the closest evidence that would come to touching on this issue is in the far right box, Your Honour. We submit to the Court that on these points, based on a very careful review of Dr. Kaiser's evidence, it is not cumulative. For instance, on Gomionica, the only evidence that touches on that specifically, one might even broadly construe it, was that one witness talked about Muslim homes being destroyed in Gomionica. That is not the same as the religious properties that Mr. Kaiser would indicate destroyed. Your Honour, we would ask the Court to consider that on these very selected showings, which is only a small portion of Dr. Kaiser's overall testimony, that the Court allow it. Our review of the Blaskic case, Your Honour, is that Dr. Kaiser's testimony was important. Quite frankly, we do believe there will be a substantial hole in the case, in the Prosecution's evidence, if at least these portions of his evidence are not admitted. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers. Other than to say that we should stick to our earlier ruling, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think immediately I should say that what this deals with, of course, are pure matters of fact. This is what this witness observed, and that is the thrust of the Prosecution's submission. If you want to say anything about that, do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I am the first to admit, Your Honour, that I have not had the opportunity extensively to review the transcript or the portions of the transcript given to us yesterday, but it appears, and I stand to be corrected on this, but it appears that Dr. Kaiser went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, he says on page 10578, in October of 1995, when the ceasefire began, having been asked by UNESCO to take up the post of representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, I suppose he does attest to the facts as he saw them when he finally went to the locations at issue some years after the events at issue, but that still seems to me to partake more in the nature of expert testimony, trying to give his views on what occurred contemporaneously, not being a contemporaneous observer himself, and therefore I see no reason to separate pieces of his testimony. He is an expert. He testified as an expert in Blaskic, and I don't think there's any reason for the Court to depart from its earlier ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered this. We take into account what the Prosecution says of this, but, nonetheless, these were matters on which we ruled not very long ago. We can see no strong argument for departing from our earlier ruling, and we shall stand by it.

utterances.text: Your Honour, then if I could address as to one other outstanding -- the Court may have other outstanding items, which it indicated earlier, housekeeping and other matters, but if the Court would allow me then to turn to one last -- I would think the last evidentiary issue.
