utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, do you have copies of these or can you tell us what these are?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Without looking at the exhibit list, Your Honour, I don't think I can specifically say. If the Court would give me a moment. I believe most of them can be generally characterised, Your Honour, as HVO and HVO-HDZ documents. Exhibit 274. I think it may be easier to see on -- 274, Your Honour, is an HVO-HDZ document concerning a meeting, calling of a meeting of the Travnik Regional Community by Dario Kordic and Ignjac Kostroman, on the 10th of November, 1992. Exhibit 281 is a record of the HDZ-BiH 2nd General Assembly in Mostar. We would also ask for Exhibit 606 to be admitted, which is, again, an invitation by Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman to a meeting dated the 5th of April, 1993. Apparently the objection there had been lack of foundation. Exhibit 729.1. It's a certificate that a particular HVO soldier was wounded on the 19th of April. Again, apparently the previous objection had been lack of foundation. 943.3. Your Honour, I'm sorry. That must be a new exhibit that wasn't on mine the last time I looked at this list. It is a second report by a civil rights investigator, dated the 19th of May, 1993. It's one of the U.N. investigators sent into Central Bosnia. Exhibit 1220.2, which was a document by Marijan Skopljak, dated the 28th of September, 1993, HVO, or HDZ, if you will, document, Your Honours. It was also specifically mentioned by Mr. Elford in his testimony. Again, it's our position it's not a document separate or distinct from many, many other HVO documents that have been admitted into evidence. Finally, Exhibit 1434, which is an ECMM report dated the 7th of -- I'm sorry -- 12th of July, 1994. Although again, Your Honour, looking at this chart, seems to indicate that it's in. If it's in, it's in, obviously. The problem, Your Honour, is there were some documents that were included in Cigar's supporting material, and it was not clear whether some of these were, in fact, in evidence or not. In any event, Your Honour, we would ask the court to include and admit 274, 281, 606, 729.1, 943.3, 1220.2, and 1434, if not already admitted, and I'll leave to Ms. Somers the open-source material. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I promise to be very brief, Your Honours. Of the two binders of material, most of which were open source, the articles which are listed, I believe, would provide necessary points of information, almost all of which come from interviews either with Franjo Tudjman or with Dario Kordic himself; Mate Boban; Josip Manolic, the security services chief at one time. Subsequently -- some of these articles are written subsequent to his departure from that position. The point we try to give very briefly. We apologise. Some of it thrown together a bit too fast, and we apologise for any brevity, but just to let the Court know what the gist of it is, and these are not the whole articles we seek to introduce. If the Court takes a look at the B/C/S parts -- and we'll clean this up considerably if the Court is so interested in having these materials -- there are just some points that are highlighted, and these would be the only points that we think would be of particular relevance. If the Court wishes to see these further, because these were -- except for number 1 and number 3, which are written in 1996 and 1998, the rest are written close in time during the time of the conflict, very much relevant in terms of time frame to the issues that have been raised in the Prosecution's case. Again, we are only seeking to have -- I must point out to the Court that there are some obituary notices that were taken from the Croatian newspapers, and the explanation is the content of it distinguishes between soldiers dying in Bosnia and soldiers dying in Croatia, HV soldiers. We would have to make sure this is cleaned up so the Court can have an accurate translation of all the different obituaries. And I just want again to the court that these are all Croatian publications -- Globus, Nacional -- either Croatian or Croatian orientation, if it's from the Bosnian Croat section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, this is the binder we have, Z2817.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just begin, Mr. President, by saying this puts us in a little bit of a difficult position. As I'm sure the Court knows, we've got substantial obligations that could be argued to fall due a week from now, and we still don't know what the evidence in the case is. We really do need to have closure on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this is why we're ruling now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Exactly. Let me just turn to the exhibits themselves. I don't have them before me, and I did not realise that these issues were going to be raised, but insofar as Exhibits Z274 and 281 are concerned, our objections are noted on the list that was delivered to us today, the OTP exhibit list, which consists of about -- well, of 68 pages. I have no idea what the numerical count on these exhibits is, but our objections are stated there. Exhibit 606, if I might just draw the Court's attention to page 29, is not even listed, so I don't even know what Exhibit 606 is. Exhibit 729.1, we've stated our objection, as recorded by the Prosecution. Exhibit 943.3. Let me say that we registered no objection to that. So that appears to be non-controversial. Exhibit 1220.2 on page 52, our objection is that there's a missing translation, but I have, I must confess, some recollection of this issue coming up, and maybe it is this document, a translation having been provided. If it has been provided, then obviously the basis for our objection would be withdrawn. If it has not been provided, then the question has to be posed: When will it be provided? And that's a real problem for us, along the lines that I just mentioned, and I'll get into that in just a minute. Exhibit 1434, I think that we registered no objection to that, and that's accurately recorded in the Prosecution's chart. With respect to this new binder of so-called open-source materials, might I just draw the Court's attention to the very first one, because I think this is representative of the general objection that we would make. It appears to be an article from Globus in 1996, and if you return to the translation of it -- I mean, the article goes on for some four pages -- there are translations of snippets, extracts taken from this article, and we believe that's not fair. If the article is to be admitted, then all of it should be admitted and there should be a translation of all of it so that we can understand what the article says, what its context is, and where the snippets that have been extracted from it stand in regard to that overall context. And I think that objection adheres generally to the articles in here, which apparently have all been translated, or at least the ones that I can flip through right now, just in part and not in whole. With respect to the other documents that the Prosecution mentioned, I really can't locate them in here. Obituary note -- maybe these are them. Provided there is an accurate translation provided of these obituaries, as the Court stated in its previous rulings, they appeared as they are in the press. Presumably they're factually founded. But the general problem is the lack of translations of these substantial number of articles and only partial translations having been provided. This is not a new issue, Mr. President, and I must confess it is somewhat surprising that it arises on the last day of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would join what my colleague said, but I would add, relating to those Prosecution open-source materials where we are dealing with press articles, here we are having a couple of interviews or similar statements of either top politicians or intelligence officers, or better to say head intelligent officers of Croatian at that time, in the press at a contemporary time. I think all of us are very well educated and experienced persons to understand that no politician, particularly an intelligence officer, would relay anything which is near to true publicly at the time of such critical events. So I really don't think there is any probative value of what either Mr. Tudjman, or Mr. Manolic, or anybody else listed here, would say to the public at that time. In addition, I notice another piece of information here. Those are announcements about deceased persons from the newspaper. I should just say that it is a national custom in Croatia and Bosnia, and other ex-Yugoslav countries, to print obituaries, which are paid, so those are informations either by family, or by friend, or some third party, or anything else. So it is also not relevant information, because there were examples -- and perhaps we will deal with that in the Defence case, if necessary -- there were many examples where, for various reasons, the friends, or families, or somebody else, announced on many occasions that somebody is supposedly dead, including location of the death, or without that including the time, or without that, for many, many different reasons, which I will obviously not enter into now. But I do not think that a page from a Croatian newspaper with such announcements has any probative value, because if such person was dead -- we have heard the testimony the citizens at that time were provided with so-called unique registering numbers of the citizen and appropriate numbers that authorities could search by computer through the official books and find out whether somebody passed away or whether somebody survived. But if that is the information which we will enter into the case, then probably we will have to show you, through the Defence case, just merely as a matter of example, that such things are simply not reliable. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I have a question to Mr. Scott just about the usefulness of -- what use are you going to make with these articles? Are you going to rely on these articles somewhere, or what is your aim in asking the Chamber to admit these newspaper articles in the evidence? Because this can help us, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To answer the Court's question, we would expect to rely on them, to various extents, as public statements by some, in many instances, senior public officials of places like the State of Croatia, which we think is corroborated by other evidence in the case. I don't think any of us would expect the Court to base a ruling, in its entirety, on a press statement. But to the extent the Court, based on the extensive evidence you've heard over the past 11 months, is able to accept -- to review these media materials in a way that, whether they are corroborated or consistent with the other evidence the Court has heard or not, are they consistent with ECMM assessments, are they consistent with what BritBat and UNPROFOR were saying, are they consistent with what other witnesses have said, the Court is in a perfect position to assess the weight that should be given to these articles. They are no different, again, than the numerous meeting material that the Court has accepted before. All the objections go to weight. As to other issues, Your Honour, there is not new material and it is not fair to say that this is yet another new set of materials. These materials were provided last fall. They've been in the Defence possession for a long, long time. As to translation issues, Your Honour, the only thing we can commit to that, as we've committed before -- and we understand the Court's ruling on other exhibits -- is that we fully understand that ultimately, and before the Court can consider these documents for purposes of judgement, they will have to be translated. We fully understand that, and we will translate them at the earliest time. I would think they could be certainly translated by early in the Defence case. The Defence will have ample opportunity to meet this evidence, ample opportunity, and we think the objections go to weight and it should be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I deal first with the single exhibits; 274, 281, 729 are all matters which are objected to, but the objections go to the weight, as we've often said before. They will be admitted. Similarly, 943.3 and 134, where there is no objection, they will be admitted. The other two documents: 606, it's said, has not been provided; and 1220.2, it's said, there's no translation. Those documents will only be admitted if they have been provided and there is a translation available. If neither of those criteria are met, why then, they won't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I haven't finished. The other application is in relation to 2817, the press materials. We have had to make a judgement about this. It seems that this evidence suffers from a number of drawbacks, if I can put it that way. First of all, the probative value, it may be, of a press article is, on occasion, open to question, and we are particularly concerned as to whether this has any real probative value. Secondly, there are the problems of translation, which are real ones. It means that the Defence are not in a position really to deal with these articles without a translation being provided. We are not satisfied that the death notices, the obituaries, have any real probative value, and of course if only extracts are translated and not the whole document, there are real difficulties both for the Defence and, of course, for the Tribunal. We are not prepared to admit these documents at this stage. If they become relevant during the course of the Defence case, of course, they can be put to witnesses or, indeed, they can be introduced during the case in rebuttal. But at this stage, because of those variety of reasons, we shan't admit 2817.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my apologies for interrupting you. I just wanted to point out that with respect to Exhibit 606, it was not our position that this document had not been provided. I simply do not know whether it has been provided, because it is not listed on the summary of outstanding exhibits that we were given by the Prosecution today. But assuming that it requires a translation and a translation is provided, obviously we would have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That brings us finally to the -- Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Mr. President. We began the hearing this morning raising the question of the international armed conflict, referring to a document which was, according to the Defence, redacted, and you asked for information on that point. I am prepared to do so, if you want me to. I've got the document with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is the position, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is the one which was referenced Z2436. It's a report dated 6 August 1993, and it comes from the Human Rights Centre of the United Nations in Zagreb. The document is being produced as we have it. No redaction was done by us. But I would like to point out that the document has five pages, and it says on the first page that there are five pages. It's also indicated, at the bottom of the last paragraph of that document on the first page, that the drafter did not attach some parts of the report in order to avoid revealing the identity of its source. So this comes right from reading the document and shows us that some information is not there, but the report is complete and it's in the state that we received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Lopez-Terres. That -- unless, Mr. Sayers, you want to say something about that particular document, I mean the explanation. It's one thing if it's redacted by the Prosecutor, but it's the document as they've received it. It doesn't seem to me that they can do much better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think it bears any further attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The matter will be admitted. Now, it's one o’clock. We are really close to the end of the matters. There are just one or two housekeeping matters which we have to consider, and the Defence want to raise something with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Three short matters ex parte. It would not take more than five minutes in total, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just deal, Mr. Scott, with the housekeeping matters. First of all, the transcripts. Now, we understand that they've been marked up by the Prosecution and they are with the Defence. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Some, as Mr. Nice I think has been indicating, Your Honour, some have been marked. I can't say that they've all been marked yet. Admittedly, we've all been busy these last couple of weeks, and some of us have been marking transcripts when we had a few extra minutes to do it ourselves. But I would expect that they could all be finished in the week ahead, given the additional time to devote to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, right. So that there's no doubt about it, perhaps you could do it within a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Within the week, because we need to start work on them ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that you just raised an additional question. We should need probably -- I'm talking about merely technical reasons in order to avoid the later problems. We should have some kind of list index of the transcripts involved, and most of those witnesses in that manner tendered in this case should get some pseudonym from this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that is a point which I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no, you're quite right to raise it, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's deal with that point now while it's still being considered. Some of the witnesses, Mr. Scott, it's right should have pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where they had pseudonyms before, unless there's any objection, they should have them again. I'll be informed of what a suitable pseudonym for a transcript is. "T1", "T2", "T3" is the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That would be possible, and I'm literally thinking about this for the first time as I stand here. It might be easier reference, in referring to the Blaskic transcripts, just to simply keep the existing designation in those and make some indication, "/B" for Blaskic, or "/K" for Kupreskic, or something, and then if someone knows they are talking about Witness NN from the Blaskic case, it's still "NN." As I said, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We needn't rule on this now, but provided it doesn't confuse the witnesses in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's the issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, some suitable form of pseudonyming should be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And, indeed, an index. I imagine there will be. An index should be prepared, indicating the witnesses whose transcripts have been admitted, together with their pseudonyms and paginated in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We appreciate that, and the points are obviously well taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and in binders, please. Yes. Now, when do the Defence think that they might be able to add any comments to the transcripts, or would you rather simply leave it, leave it be and leave it for comment? It may be simpler, given the time constraints, for you to simply comment on the transcripts in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour. But just thinking out loud, it might be useful for us to supply the particular parts upon which we would rely in due course, and I can't say exactly when that would be because we have some pretty substantial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is this: that we will receive the Prosecution transcripts, marked up, indicating the parts on which they rely, and the Defence can deal with it in whatever way they think fit. It may be appropriate, during the Defence case, for you to produce those parts upon which you rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's appropriate. But let me say just one thing on this, Your Honour. We're concerned that there's a little bit of a moving target here. We've got a very short period of time within which to prepare a fairly substantial document, and we really don't know what the, you know, the final state of the evidence is. And I frankly am at a loss to know how to assess that. If we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You now should know what's been admitted and what hasn't. Have you the transcripts which have been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you've got the evidence, and you should have all the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Except for the translations, which are still to be provided, and that's -- might we suggest -- I don't know that there's a substantial number of translations that are outstanding. Might we suggest that a deadline be set for them, you know, by Monday or Tuesday, and that maybe our one week to do the motion for judgement of acquittal runs from that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're concerned not to let the timetable slip. When can we expect any outstanding translations? I know there are translation problems, but this is a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid the honest answer to that is I can't begin to anticipate. As you know, those resources are entirely outside of our control. We have a number of matters pending. We have asked and we have submitted translation requests, but I think it would be disingenuous for me to stand here and try to give you some prediction. I don't know, without talking to them and asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The simplest course may be this: that if you are going to rely on any untranslated documents in your submissions, then they will have to be translated. If you're not going to rely on any untranslated documents, then the matter may not be so pressing. If, Mr. Sayers, you come across documents which you need for the purposes of your submissions, then you can refer the matter to us in writing while we're not sitting, and we'll deal with it as best we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could I raise one more -- I hate to be the -- well, it's on the international armed conflict issue. The Court has requested, in its ruling of March the 8th, submissions from the Prosecution within two weeks, and then requested submissions from us two weeks after that, and we're pleased to make submissions. But it's difficult for me to see exactly what we would be responding to without introducing our own evidence on the subject. Did the Court have in mind us highlighting particular issues which would be disputed and particular issues which would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If it wasn't clear, it should be, that what the Trial Chamber wants is the matters at this stage that are in dispute, what it is you dispute about their submissions; not your positive case, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That will be no problem, Your Honour, and thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the other outstanding matters which the Chamber needs are the village binders, in their final form, and the final list of exhibits. Admittedly, that will have to reflect our rulings today. Is there any reason why those should not be with the Trial Chamber within seven days?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Subject to Ms. Verhaag, Your Honour, I can't see why that shouldn't be doable by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the important point is we have it and the Defence have it in order to deal with any submissions that are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the order will be seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, if the Court will allow me just three final housekeeping matters, if you will, from the Prosecution side. First off, Your Honour, as to the marking of the transcripts, I feel compelled to tell the Court, so there is no misunderstanding, in marking some of the transcripts to date, when you get to a village witness whose transcript may be 40 pages in direct and it's all about the attack on Han Ploca, for instance, I wouldn't want the Court to think that you necessarily be more selective than one would expect. I mean that witness tells the story about the attack on Han Ploca, and it isn't a question of saying, "Well, we want this one line here and one line on the next page." I mean obviously it's the story of that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A broad indication is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour -- I guess it's a request to the Defence, if you will, through the Court, or if the Court has any feelings on it, the Court could give some guidance -- it would be helpful to the Prosecution, Your Honour, if the Defence might consider giving us their half time or motions for judgement of acquittal in electronic form. If they would consider doing that, it might assist making a timely response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any difficulty about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't anticipate any difficulty, but if there is, we'll promptly notify the Chamber and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution in particular. It seems sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, Mr. Nice mentioned this yesterday, but I do feel -- this is very important in Prosecution, and it's a matter of some point to us. We will, if you will, rest our case with the outstanding binding order litigation in mind. We are fully of a mind, Your Honour, that if the various parties, the Federation or Croatia, are in fact prepared finally to be forthright in the production of documents, that there could be very important documents that would still be important to bring to the Court's attention. To the extent we rest, Your Honour, we rest subject to the ability to bring those documents before the Court, documents which have been asked now for some three-plus years. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We understand that that is the Prosecution case, that you're reserving your position on any future documentation which may appear, and we will consider that in due course and the appropriate course to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will hear the Defence ex parte motion now. Meanwhile, as far as the general case is concerned, it's adjourned until the next hearing, which will be on the 30th of March, at the usual time, half past 9. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of March, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
